# Review and Save Project Memory

This rule applies to the main agent. The project memory system is chosen at setup and recorded in `.toolkit.json`; with built-in memory it is the local `.memory/` folder. It is the single project memory store. Claude's native auto-memory and the `claude-toolkit` Second Brain plugin are disabled for this project. The session-start briefing shows the current focus in Claude Code and Codex. Do not treat a hook reminder as a save decision.

## Decide the destination first

Read the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory) and the likely owning record. Send current focuses, owner to-dos, and handoff context to the current focus; sourced terminology to the glossary; qualifying otherwise-unowned durable context to a topic; active work to the chosen tracker; decisions for the whole project to `DECISIONS.md`; accepted delivered behavior to requirements; the technical approach to the design kept with its work item; verified current structure to the System Guide; and repeatable procedure to instructions or a skill. Raw external documentation stays in its source folder. A small memory pointer can route future sessions to a hard-to-find authority without copying its body.

Review on explicit remember/forget requests, corrections, standing preferences, meaningful decisions or discoveries, significant fixes or episodes, people/tool/reference changes, focus shifts, work-item completion, and handoffs. The toolkit's `UserPromptSubmit` hook flags only explicit keep phrases, and its Stop hook checks once per turn that such a phrase was handled. Do not save on every hook reminder or every turn. A review can end with no memory.

## Approval

The `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy: what the owner's own words authorize, what needs a yes in onboarding mode, what trusted mode allows, and what always needs the owner. The mode is `memory.approval` in `.toolkit.json`; only an explicit owner instruction changes it. A yes authorizes the shown operation and meaning only. Silence does not. An unanswered save question is kept as a proposal: the agent does not rely on it, and `work-decide` shows it to the owner until he approves or rejects it. The `memory-save` skill says how.

If the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it. Save only a general selection rule, as a `feedback` memory, if their feedback supplies one; do not restate the rejected fact in the current focus or another topic. Review similar candidates against that rule from then on.

## Saving and completion

The main agent saves memory itself through the `memory-save` skill, which runs `toolkit memory` commands; there is no curator agent. Search first with `toolkit memory find`, then save with `toolkit memory save`, retire with `toolkit memory retire`, and write the current focus or glossary with `toolkit memory focus --set-file` or `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. The commands lock memory, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index.

For a focus-only change or already-authorized glossary maintenance, save without a lasting-memory question. Several independent signals can be grouped into one save; do not run parallel writes against the same topic or index. Before claiming a save succeeded, read it back with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor`; tell the user briefly what was retained or what needs a decision.
# Write Artifacts in Plain English

An artifact is something an agent generates for a person to look at: a
diagram, a chart, a dashboard, a visualization, a mockup, a slide deck, a
published page, or a generated document. This rule is about the words inside
one: the title, the headings, the labels, the notes, the captions, the body
text.

The project's output style says how the agent talks in chat. The words inside
an artifact follow the same style. This rule exists because the output style
reaches only the main chat: a helper agent, a skill, or a Codex session that
makes an artifact never sees it. Read the active style file when there is
one. Where this rule and that file differ, the style file wins.

## Write about the subject

Every word describes the thing the artifact shows. The reader opened it to
learn about that thing, not about the artifact or the conversation that
produced it.

- Do not narrate the artifact. "Here is where the change lands, but only the
  key pieces" says nothing about the system. Cut it, or say what changed.
- Do not tell the reader what matters. "Here is the load-bearing decision"
  tells them how to feel. Write the decision.
- Bring in the conversation only when it is the fact. A quote earns its place
  when the exact words are what the reader needs, and then it says who said
  it and when. A quote the reader cannot place is noise.

## A heading names what is under it

A heading is a label, not a hook. It says what the reader is about to look
at, in the words of the subject.

The four headings below are an example: a page of options for who can see and
edit which projects in a team web app. The left column sells the section; the
right column names it.

| Written | Say instead |
|---|---|
| Three ways to build the team tree, pick one | Team structure options |
| One question decides the whole shape | Decision: can a team lead edit their own team's projects? |
| Four facts that rule out the most obvious answers | How team access works |
| What shape actually hands to a real person | Project visibility by role |

A number belongs in a heading when the number is the fact: "Three departments
share one role". "Three ways to build it" only counts the section below, and
the reader can count.

## Use the real name

Call a thing what the system calls it, every time. In that example the real
names are team structure, project visibility, sharing rule, admin access, and
permission group. The page used picture words instead: "shape" for the team
structure, "lever" for a setting, "leaks" for access people should not have,
"flows up" for a manager getting access to their team's projects. That is
figurative language, and it is not allowed. It makes the reader translate, and
a reader who does not know the system cannot.

A term the reader may not know gets a plain definition the first time it
appears. After that, the term is used unchanged.

A box or label carries the real name. Anything it needs to say about itself
is one plain line.

## Say the plain thing

Use the active output style inside the artifact. This artifact rule also requires:

- Common words. Short sentences. One idea each.
- No figurative or metaphorical language. No idioms, no jokes, no picture word
  standing in for a real thing.
- No preamble. Start with the content.
- No closing line that sums up or cheers.
- Fewer words, never fewer facts. Every number, name, date, and quotation
  stays exactly as it is.

## What this rule does not decide

How the artifact is laid out: how many boxes, what an arrow says, where a
note goes, whether there is a key. Every artifact is different, and the agent
making it decides. This rule decides the words.
# Prepare a Session Handoff

When the owner says he is clearing context or ending the session, or asks for a handoff, use the `handoff` skill, whatever the session's length. When the session is long and the next step is complex, offer a handoff. Use the `handoff` skill. Before the handoff, review the current focus (`toolkit memory focus`) and the memory criteria; update the focus, and save only authorized lasting memory, with the `memory-save` skill. Then write the prompt. Skip the offer for small edits and quick lookups.
# Work Safely in a Shared Repository

Other sessions edit this repository now. Before your first edit, run:

```
git worktree list
git status
git fetch origin && git log --oneline -10
```

- No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): skip `git fetch`, and never report a fetch failure as a blocker.
- An unknown worktree, moved branch, or change you did not make means other sessions are live. Do not fix it. Tell the owner.
- Code, rules, skills, hooks, settings: use your own worktree and branch (`git worktree add .claude/worktrees/<name> -b claude/<name>`). Exception: a one-file edit asked for directly.
- Documentation-only saves: open the `publish-docs` skill.
- In the shared primary checkout, never switch branches, reset, rebase, or stash.
- Never touch another session's branch or uncommitted work.
- Stage paths by name. Never `git add -A`, `git add .`, or `git commit -a`. Read the full staged diff.
- Never hand-edit a generated file.
- Before taking a sequential number, check every tracker folder, worktree, and the remote. On a later collision, renumber only your own.
- Land implementation by pull request, merged with the owner's approval. A standing merge instruction the owner gave for this project counts.
- Before a merge, compare `git diff --name-only <default-branch>...<branch>` with `git status` in the primary checkout. A file in both: stop, name it, ask the owner.
- After the merge, remove your worktree and branch.
# Local Work-Item Folders

This project tracks work in local folders under `.work-items/`. The folder is
Git-ignored, lives in the main checkout, and is shared by every worktree. It is
not backed up by Git: `toolkit export` is the backup.

## An item is found by its ID, not its path

- An item is a folder holding a record, `WORK-ITEM.md`, and `DESIGN.md` when a
  design exists. The frontmatter `id` (for example `WI-001`) is the item's
  identity. The folder name and the file name may change.
- Refer to items by ID everywhere. Find an item's files with
  `toolkit work show <id> --path`. Never guess a path.
- Create items only with `toolkit work new`. It takes the next ID under a lock,
  so parallel sessions never pick the same one. IDs are never reused.

## The owner may move folders, and the agent adapts

- The owner may move, rename, nest, or group item folders by hand. That is
  normal. `toolkit work sync` finds every item again by its ID; the session
  hooks and every `toolkit work` command run it. Report what moved and continue.
  Use the `work-organize` skill to reconcile anything the sync reports as
  missing or duplicated.
- A record inside another item's folder is that item's sub-item: its `parent`
  follows its location. A plain folder with no record is a group and changes no
  parent.
- `archive/` is a reserved group. Items there are hidden from the briefing and
  from `toolkit work next`.
- Never move, group, archive, or rename items on your own initiative. When the
  owner asks, use `toolkit work move <id> --under <id|group|archive|root>`.

## What the tracker ignores, and what it generates

- Ignored: `work-item-template/`, any folder whose name starts with `_` or `.`,
  and any record whose title is still `<Work item title>`.
- Generated by `toolkit work sync`: `DASHBOARD.md`. State kept by `toolkit work`:
  `.toolkit-state.json` (the ID-to-path map and the highest ID used). Never edit
  either by hand.
- Change frontmatter fields (stage, status, parent, waiting on, approvals) only
  with `toolkit work` commands. Body sections may be edited directly or with
  `toolkit work edit`; the hook checks the record after each edit.
- Keep any other files the owner put in an item folder.

# Work decide

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Walks the owner through what waits on him, one decision at a time, and records each answer where it belongs. Track these steps with the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

## Steps

1. Build the queue. The command lists each decision once: requirements waiting for approval, proposed designs, results at stage 11, Open Questions rows the owner decides, and memory proposals. Its "Agent to-do" lines are not decisions. A delivery offer belongs to `work-delegate`: open it after his other decisions.
   `toolkit work decisions`
2. He gave an answer without being asked ("approved", "go with B"): match it to exactly one waiting decision; when two could match, ask which, naming both. A bare "yes", "ok", or "looks good" with no question asked is not an answer (`references/approvals.md`, section 1).
3. Otherwise start with the count and one short line for every waiting decision, memory proposals included ("3 decisions wait on you: the WI-004 design, the WI-006 result, and a memory proposal about deploy days."). Then take them one at a time, the one blocking the most work first: what is decided, the choices, your recommendation and its main reason, and what happens after each answer. One decision per message, in the reply text.
4. An approval: read the item, then run that gate's checklist in `references/approvals.md` (requirements: section 2; design: section 3; result: section 4).
   `toolkit work show <id>`
5. An Open Questions answer: save his words first, rewrite that row with the answer, the date, and Answered, then set `waiting_on` back (`references/recording-owner-answers.md`, sections 4 and 5).
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner said: <quote>' --effect '<what the answer changes>'`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Open Questions' --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
6. A memory proposal: show its one line and your recommendation. Yes: approve it. No: reject it, and never propose the same fact again (`references/proposals.md`).
   `toolkit memory approve <key> --by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory reject <key>`
7. A decision for the whole project: add the row inside the `publish-docs` save workspace, in the order in `references/decisions-log.md`.
   `toolkit decision add --decision '<decision>' --why '<why>' --by <owner>`
8. A "no" or a change: record it as the answer, move the item back (for example to refinement), and open the skill that redoes the work.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
9. Lead with "Not saved" if any write failed. Update the current focus when an answer changed an item's next step (`references/current-focus.md`). Empty queue: say so and offer `work-on` for unblocked items. End with the next decision's question or the exact words that continue.

## Gotchas

- Run each `toolkit` command alone: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). One-line values go in single quotes, never double quotes; an apostrophe inside them is `'\''` in Claude Code and ’ (U+2019) in Codex, or reword the text. Section text goes on standard input (`--set-file -`) in Claude Code, and in `--text '<text>'` or a `mktemp -d` file in Codex (`references/toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
- Every decision carries a recommendation, even when it is the only one in the queue. A bare question is not enough.
- Ask in the reply text, never through a question tool.
- The approve command marks the Open Questions rows that asked for it Answered and prints "Marked Q-xx Answered". Never edit those rows again by hand.
- `waiting_on`: `agent` when the agent continues, `none` when nothing waits, `owner` while another of his questions on that item is still open. The approve command sets `none` by itself.
- A memory proposal is not a fact until he approves it. Do not rely on it.
- An approval never covers merge, deployment, spending, or publishing.
- After a result approval, the item continues with `work-finish`. Open it when he wants it shipped now.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Build the queue from the labels in `references/tracker-github.md` or `references/tracker-jira.md`, and remove the waiting-on-owner label after each approval or last answer.

## Example decision message

```markdown
WI-015 needs your choice of design.

- Option A: use the built-in report page. Ready in about a day; the layout is fixed.
- Option B: a custom page. About a week; any layout you want.

I recommend A, because every requirement is met without custom code.
After A: I plan the build. After B: I plan a longer build and ask you about the layout.

Do you approve Option A?
```

# Work organize

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Explains what the owner changed in the tracker, asks only where his intent is unclear, and splits or moves items when he asks; it never moves anything on its own. Track these steps with the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

## Steps

1. Rescan the tracker, then read the tree and the report: moved, renamed, nested or un-nested, archived, missing, duplicate id, adopted.
   `toolkit work sync`
   `toolkit work list --tree`
2. Say each report line to the owner, one line each, before other work (`references/moves.md`, section 1). The CLI already wrote the history rows.
3. Ask about each case that needs his intent, one at a time, with your recommendation: a missing or trashed item, a duplicate id, a sub-item under a finished parent, an item marked Done by hand, a skipped gate (`references/moves.md`, section 2).
   `toolkit work cancel <id> --reason '<his words>'`
4. Split (stage 05): propose the sub-items, ask once, then create each child with `--covers` for the parent requirements it delivers, and update the parent's Roadmap, with the checklist in `references/moves.md`, section 3.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 05-breakdown`
   `toolkit work new --title '<title>' --type <type> --parent <id> --covers R-02,R-03`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section Roadmap --set-file <file>`
5. Nest, group, move, archive, or restore only when the owner asks. First say how many nested items move with it (`references/moves.md`, section 4).
   `toolkit work move <id> --under <target>`
6. Validate, show a short tree of what changed, and add a history note only for the owner's reason.
   `toolkit work validate`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Moved because the owner asked: <his words>'`
7. Update the current focus when a split or a move changed an item's next step (`references/current-focus.md`). one. Run each checklist in order; one wrong or missing command leaves the

## 1. What counts as approval

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the gates and these rules. In short:

- Only the owner's explicit words count. Quote them in a history note.
- A question, a suggestion, a tentative answer ("probably B"), silence, or a
  saved draft is not approval.
- An approval covers only what was shown. It never covers merge, deployment,
  spending, or publishing.
- An approval survives later stages. A stage alone does not prove approval:
  check the approval field (`toolkit work show <id>`).
- A bare "yes", "ok", or "looks good" answers only a yes-or-no question asked
  earlier in this conversation. When none was asked, or the waiting question
  is not a yes-or-no question, show the decision with its choices and your
  recommendation, and record nothing.
- After a yes, save his words first, in a history note that starts with
  `Owner said:`. Then run the gate's commands. A command that refuses then
  never loses his answer, and no later session asks him again.

| The owner says | After this question | It is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "Yes, approved." | "Do you approve these requirements?" | The requirements approval |
| "Go with B." | The design options with a recommendation | The choice and approval of Option B |
| "Looks good." | "Do you approve this result?" | The result approval |
| "Looks good." | "Shall I split WI-12 into these three sub-items?" | A yes to the split only, not a result approval |
| "ok" | Nothing was asked in this chat | Not an answer; ask what he wants |
| "Probably A, but let me think." | The design options | Not an answer; the design stays proposed |
| "Ship it." | He has seen the result, gaps, and evidence | The result approval (record it with his words) |

## 2. Requirements approval

Asked by `work-requirements`. `work-decide` records a later answer.

Before asking:

- [ ] The Agreed goal holds real text. The CLI refuses the approval while it
      still holds the template text.
- [ ] The spec check ran (`requirements-analyst`), and its findings were fixed
      or turned into questions.
- [ ] No Open Questions row linked to a requirement is still open. If one is,
      say which and ask it first.

Ask: show the Agreed goal, each requirement in one line, the Acceptance list,
and any open question. Then ask exactly "Do you approve these requirements?"
as the last line, and set the item waiting on the owner.

```text
toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner
```

After his yes, in this order:

- [ ] Save his words first, so no later session asks him again.
      `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner said: <quote>' --effect 'Requirements approved.'`
- [ ] Set each approved `R-xx` Status to Finalized and add who approved it and
      when to its Decision record, in one edit of `Active requirements`.
      `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Active requirements' --set-file <file>`
- [ ] Record the approval. It adds its own history row, marks the Open
      Questions rows that asked for it Answered, sets `waiting_on` to `none`,
      and moves an earlier item to stage 03.
      `toolkit work approve <id> --requirements --by <owner>`
- [ ] Hand the item back to the agent, unless another question for him is
      still open on it.
      `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
- [ ] Check the record.
      `toolkit work validate <id>`
- [ ] Next: a `build` or `data-load` item goes to `solution-design`, unless the
      owner agreed to skip the design. Say a skip in the final reply, not in a

Not yet, or a change: the item stays waiting on him. Record the change and
ask again.

A yes that arrives later (`work-decide` records it):

- The Agreed goal still holds the template text: write the goal he was shown
  with the approval question, then record the approval.
  `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Agreed goal' --text '<goal he was shown>'`
- A requirement still has a linked open question: say which one, open
  `work-requirements` for it, and record the approval once it is answered,

After his yes, or his choice of one option, in this order:

- [ ] Save his words first, so no later session asks him again.

- [ ] The tests and every acceptance check ran, and an independent checker

- [ ] The check is recorded in a history note (what was checked, the
      evidence, the gaps).
- [ ] The item is at stage 11 and waits on the owner. Add no Open Questions

## 5. Done

Asked by `work-finish`. Only `toolkit work finish` sets Done.

Before the finish command:

- [ ] The result approval is recorded, or you have the owner's own words
      approving this result to pass with `--quote`.
- [ ] Every change the item made is committed and reached the default branch,
      or the owner said to leave it on the branch.
- [ ] Requirements and system guide updates are saved through `publish-docs`.
- [ ] Every open sub-item is finished, cancelled, or moved, or the owner said
      the parent is done anyway.
- [ ] Every Roadmap phase the item completed says Done.
- [ ] Overview: Related items current, Current position "Done on <date>:
      <evidence>", Blockers "None.".
- [ ] Leftover worktrees and branches for the item are listed and offered for
      removal.

Then run one of these:

```text
toolkit work finish <id> --by <owner> --evidence '<what shows it works>'
toolkit work finish <id> --by <owner> --evidence '<what shows it works>' --quote '<his exact words>'
toolkit work finish <id> --by <owner> --evidence '<what shows it works>' --allow-open-sub-items
```

The second is only for a result approval not yet recorded. The third is only
for a parent the owner said is done while sub-items are still open; quote his
words in a history note. The command sets Next action and Resume here, and
prints what still needs a note.

The finish command also backs up `.work-items/` and `.memory/` (and Hindsight
memory) to the owner's backup folder and prints one line about it. Read that
line:

- "Backed up ... to <folder>": done. Say it in one line in the reply.
- "No backup folder is set ...": ask the owner for a folder outside the
  project, as a question in the reply. After his answer:
  `toolkit config set backup.dir <folder>` (or `none` when he wants no backup).
- A line with "failed" or "Tell the owner": tell him that line as it is. The
  item is still Done; only the backup is missing.

Asked by `work-finish`. Only `toolkit work cancel` sets Cancelled.

- [ ] The reason is the owner's own words, not a summary.
- [ ] Each open sub-item: ask whether to cancel it, move it to the top level,
      or move it under another item. Never cancel them without asking.
- [ ] `toolkit work cancel <id> --reason '<his words>'`

Cancelling keeps the record. Nothing is deleted.

## 7. Delivery offer

Only `work-delegate` makes the offer and records the answer. Every other skill
opens `work-delegate` for it. The recorded value:

```text
toolkit work set <id> --delivery agent-led
toolkit work set <id> --delivery owner-led
```

A delivery answer never approves requirements, a design, or a result, and
never widens merge, deployment, spending, or publishing.

## 8. Project-wide decision

Recorded by `work-decide` as a row in `DECISIONS.md` at the project root,
then committed through `publish-docs`.

```text
toolkit decision add --decision '<decision>' --why '<why>' --by <owner>
toolkit decision add --decision '<decision>' --why '<why>' --by <owner> --replaces D-<n>
```

`DECISIONS.md` is append-only. A changed decision is a new row that names the
one it replaces. Any skill that meets a project-wide decision opens
`work-decide`, which runs the full order of work with `publish-docs`.

## 9. Memory proposal

A memory the owner did not answer ("Save to memory?") is saved as a proposal:
status `needs-review`. The agent does not rely on it until he approves it.

```text
toolkit memory approve <key> --by <owner>
toolkit memory reject <key>
```

A rejection deletes the proposal. Never propose the same fact again in other
words.

## 10. Sub-items and approvals

- A child made with `--covers R-02,R-03` links those parent requirements and
  inherits the parent's requirements approval. The owner is never asked to
  approve the same requirement twice.
- A parent design the owner approved covers its `--covers` children: they
  start at planning (stage 06) with no design of their own.
- A child that needs new behavior gets its own `R-xx` and its own approval.
- Each sub-item needs its own result approval. The owner's approval of the
  parent does not cover it.
- Finishing a sub-item never finishes or approves its parent.

## 11. Standing merge instruction

A merge normally needs the owner's yes to that merge. A standing merge
instruction replaces that yes only when all of these hold:

- [ ] `DECISIONS.md` records it as the owner's decision (the project's
      `AGENTS.md` may point at it);
- [ ] an `acceptance-checker` that did not build the change reported no
      blocking issue on that exact head commit;
- [ ] every check passes on that head;
- [ ] the work item does not say its merge needs the owner's approval (an
      item that says so overrides the instruction).

Without an independent check the instruction does not apply: ask the owner.
A new commit after the check means a new check on the new head.

## 12. When an approve command refuses

- Show the owner the command's error in plain words. Never work around it by
  editing the record, the design text, or a header field.
- The error names what is missing (for example the Agreed goal still holds
  the template text). Fix that, then run the same command again.
- Exit code 2 means a refused gate: the record is unchanged.

Run these in order.

- [ ] Set the split stage.
      `toolkit work set <id> --stage 05-breakdown`
- [ ] Propose the sub-items in one message: for each, a title, what it
      delivers, which of the parent's `R-xx` it covers, and which phase of

- [ ] Ask once: "Shall I split WI-12 into these three sub-items?"

      approved parent requirements names them with `--covers`: it links them,

# The current focus

Purpose: the format of the current focus, when to change it, and the exact
read-change-save sequence, in every memory backend.

## Contents

- What the focus is for
- The format
- What goes in each section
- When to check it
- Read, change, save
- A new project's focus
- Examples
- Checklist for a focus save

## What the focus is for

The current focus is the first thing the next session reads: the session
briefing includes it. It says what is happening now and where the next
session starts. It never repeats the tracker: a work item's status, tasks,
and history stay in the work item.

| Backend | Where the focus lives |
| --- | --- |
| Built-in | `.memory/CURRENT_FOCUS.md` in the main checkout |
| Hindsight | The document `focus` in the project's bank |
| Notion | The "Current focus" page under the project's page |

The same commands read and save it in every backend. Never edit the file or
the page by hand.

## The format

The model's format: a `# Current focus` title line, a `Last updated:` line,
then exactly four `##` sections in this order, under 50 lines in total.

```markdown
# Current focus

Last updated: <YYYY-MM-DD>, <source>, <person or agent>

## Now

## Waiting on the owner

## Untracked to-dos

## Next session starts with
```

What the command enforces:

- It refuses a focus that lacks one of the four sections, has another
  section, or is over 50 lines (exit code 2, nothing saved).
- It adds the title line or the `Last updated:` line when either is missing,
  and sets an older date to today. It cannot know the source or who wrote
  it, so write the line yourself.

## What goes in each section

- **Last updated:** the date, the source (for example `handoff`,
  `work-finish`, `chat`), and who wrote it (a person, or `agent`). Change it
  on every save.
- **Now:** the current outcome or area, with work item ids and titles only,
  for example `- WI-012 CSV export`. Never a status or a stage: the tracker
  holds those.
- **Waiting on the owner:** a decision or action only the owner can take
  that has no work item: what it is, who needs it, and when to check again.
  Work items that wait on him are listed by `toolkit work decisions`, not
  here. A setup step (trust the hooks in Codex, sign in to Notion with
  `ntn login`) stays only while `toolkit doctor` still reports it.
- **Untracked to-dos:** things the owner asked for that have no work item.
  When one becomes a work item, replace the line with the item's id under
  Now.
- **Next session starts with:** one entry: where to resume, what to read,
  and the next action. It is replaced at each handoff, not added to.
- Write "None." in a section with nothing in it.
- Keep it under 50 lines by replacing stale lines, never by appending. Never
  drop an owner to-do that is still open only to meet the limit.

## When to check it

Check the focus before the reply ends when:

- a work item's stage changes, or its next step changes to something the
  focus does not say. Check two things:
  1. Now lists the item (id and title). Add it when it is missing; take it
     off when the item is Done or Cancelled.
  2. Next session starts with does not name a step that is done or no longer
     next. Replace that line with the item's real next step, in one line that
     points at the item, for example "Continue WI-012 from its Resume here:
     build P1."
- the owner asks for something with no work item (add it under Untracked
  to-dos), or a decision only he can make has no work item (Waiting on the
  owner).
- `toolkit doctor` no longer reports a setup step listed under Waiting on the
  owner (drop it).
- a session hands off (replace the one entry under Next session starts
  with).

Skip the save when nothing in the focus is wrong. Leave every line you are
not changing exactly as it is.

## Read, change, save

1. Read it with its version. The output has `text` and `version`:

   ```text
   toolkit memory focus --json
   ```

2. Change only the lines that need it, in the whole text, and update the
   `Last updated:` line.
3. Save the whole text with the version you read.
   Claude Code: `<file>` is `-`, with the text on standard input after a
   quoted heredoc (`<<'EOF'`), then a line holding only `EOF`.

   ```text
   toolkit memory focus --set-file <file> --expect <version>
   ```

   Codex: give the text in single quotes instead (newlines are kept), or
   use a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder and delete it after the save.
   Write an apostrophe as ’ (the curly apostrophe, U+2019), or reword the
   text. Never `'\''` in Codex: the project's command rule does not match
   that form, so the command runs inside the sandbox, and the tool call can
   drop the backslash.

   ```text
   toolkit memory focus --text '<text>' --expect <version>
   ```

4. Exit code 2 with "changed since it was read" means another session saved
   the focus after you read it. Read it again, make your change in the new
   text, and save with the new version. Never save without `--expect`: that
   would silently drop the other session's change.
5. No focus yet (`version` is null): save with `--expect absent`, in the full
   format above.
6. Read it back:

   ```text
   toolkit memory focus
   ```

## A new project's focus

A new project's focus still holds the model's setup text: a fill-in guide
comment under the title (`<!-- Fill-in guide: ... -->`) and an
`<angle-bracket>` prompt in every section. At the first save:

- remove the fill-in guide comment;
- replace each prompt with real content, or with "None." when there is none;
- never leave an angle-bracket prompt in a saved focus.

## Examples

A full focus:

```markdown
# Current focus

Last updated: 2026-09-26, handoff, agent

## Now

- WI-012 CSV export
- WI-015 Large exports (sub-item of WI-012)

## Waiting on the owner

- Pick a hosting provider before the first deploy (no work item yet); check again 2026-10-01.

## Untracked to-dos

- Email the client about the October demo.

## Next session starts with

- 2026-09-26 17:40 UTC | CSV export: continue WI-012 from its Resume here. Goal: exports finish under 10 seconds.
```

The handoff entry with a work item is a pointer only:
`<UTC date and time> | <topic>: continue <WI-id> from its Resume here. Goal: <one line>.`

With no work item, the entry is a short note: the goal or topic, where work
stopped, the first next action, limits on what may be done without the
owner, and open questions. Do not create a work item only to hold it.

## Checklist for a focus save

- [ ] Read with `--json`; you have the version.
- [ ] The `# Current focus` title and the `Last updated:` line (date,
      source, who) are there.
- [ ] Four sections, in order; "None." in each empty one.
- [ ] Work item ids and titles only; no status or stage.
- [ ] No angle-bracket prompt and no fill-in guide comment left.
- [ ] Under 50 lines; no open owner to-do dropped.
- [ ] Saved with `--expect`; read back.

# Running `toolkit` commands

Purpose: how to run a `toolkit` command in Claude Code and in Codex, how to
pass text in one, and what each exit code means. Every skill that runs a
`toolkit` command follows this file.

## Contents

- Running toolkit commands
- Text in a command
- Exit codes
- Reporting a save
- Reading output and updating what you read
- Right and wrong examples

## Running toolkit commands

- Put each `toolkit` command on its own line and run it as a plain command,
  in both hosts. Do not join it to another command with `&&`, `;`, or a pipe,
  and do not wrap it in `$(...)`, a loop, or a script. This holds for read
  commands too: `toolkit work decisions && toolkit work show WI-001` is two
  commands, run one after the other.
- Why, in Codex: the project's command rule (`.codex/rules/toolkit.rules`)
  runs a `toolkit` command outside the sandbox only when it is the whole
  command. A `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a
  heredoc, `cd ... &&`) or run from a script (for example Python's
  `subprocess`) runs inside the Codex sandbox. The sandbox blocks Notion, the
  local Hindsight server, and the main checkout's `.work-items/` and
  `.memory/` from a worktree, so the command fails or reports the wrong
  cause.
- The one thing a Claude Code command may carry is its own text on standard
  input (`--set-file -` with a quoted heredoc; "Text in a command", below).
- Five commands ask the owner first, in both hosts, because they are hard or
  impossible to undo: `toolkit machine-setup`, `toolkit memory delete`,
  `toolkit memory import`, `toolkit import`, and
  `toolkit hindsight service install` or `start`. Get his yes in the reply
  before you run one. The host then asks him to confirm the command (Claude
  Code: a permission prompt; Codex: an approval). That prompt is expected, not
  an error.
- In Codex, run each of those five alone, with `sandbox_permissions` set to
  `require_escalated` and a one-line reason. The approval alone keeps the
  command inside the sandbox, where it fails: `toolkit memory delete` cannot
  reach Hindsight or Notion, `toolkit machine-setup` cannot write `~/.codex`
  or `~/.local/bin`, `toolkit hindsight service install` cannot write
  `~/Library/LaunchAgents`, and `toolkit import` from a worktree cannot write
  the main checkout.
- Write `--json` and `--host` after the command words
  (`toolkit memory delete <key> --owner-approved --json`). The toolkit refuses
  those five commands when a flag comes first, because the ask-first rules
  would not match them.
- Never change a work item or a memory record with a script or a shell write
  (Python, Node, `sed -i`, `cat >`, `tee`, `cp`). Use the `toolkit` command
  that owns it. The hooks refuse the shell write, so it only wastes a step.
- `toolkit help <command>` prints every option of one command.

## Text in a command

The shell changes text before the command sees it. Inside double quotes it
runs anything between backticks and anything in `$(...)` as a command, and
puts that command's output in the text. The command then saves the text with
those parts missing and still reports success. So:

- **One-line values** (`--note`, `--effect`, `--append-row`, `--title`,
  `--reason`, `--quote`, `--evidence`, `--description`, `--source`): put them
  in single quotes, in both hosts. Inside single quotes the shell changes
  nothing. Never use double quotes for text.
- **An apostrophe inside single quotes:**
  - Claude Code: write it as `'\''`, for example
    `--note 'Owner said: "it'\''s ready, ship it"'`.
  - Codex: write it as ’ (the curly apostrophe, U+2019), or reword the text.
    Never `'\''` in Codex: the command rule does not match that form, so the
    command runs inside the sandbox, and the tool call can drop the
    backslash, which leaves a quote that is never closed.
- **Section, design, focus, glossary, and memory text in Claude Code:** pass
  it on standard input with `--set-file -` (or `--body-file -` for a memory
  save) and a quoted heredoc. The quotes around `EOF` in `<<'EOF'` stop the
  shell from changing anything in the text, and no file is left anywhere.
  Claude Code refuses `rm` outside the project, so a temporary file there
  could never be deleted. Write the command, then the text, then a line
  holding only `EOF`:

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Overview' --set-file - <<'EOF'
  <the whole section text>
  EOF
  ```

- **The same text in Codex:** a heredoc runs the command inside the sandbox,
  so do not use one. Give short or medium text in single quotes
  (`--text '<text>'`; newlines inside the quotes are kept). For longer text:
  1. Make a new folder for this one save with `mktemp -d`. Its name is
     unique, so two sessions or two projects never share a file.
  2. Write the file in it with the file edit tool (`apply_patch`).
  3. Run the `toolkit` command alone, with the file's full path.
  4. Delete the file and the folder right after the command succeeds
     (`rm <file>`, then `rmdir <folder>`), before you ask the owner anything.

  Never write the file and run the `toolkit` command in one shell command.

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Overview' --text '<text>'
  toolkit work design <id> --text '<text>' --status proposed
  toolkit memory focus --text '<text>' --expect <version>
  ```

- Never use a fixed file name such as `/tmp/wi001-requirements.md`. Every
  project starts at `WI-001`, so another session's save could land in this
  item.
- Never leave a draft file inside `.work-items/` or `.memory/`. A second
  `DESIGN.md`-shaped file there confuses the design lookup, and a stray note
  in `.memory/` is read as a memory.

## Exit codes

`toolkit help work` prints them as: "0 ok, 1 error, 2 validation failure or a
refused gate, 3 not supported for this tracker, 4 not a toolkit project."
`toolkit help memory` uses the same numbers: "1 error or not found, 2 refused
(a rule or a stale --expect), 3 not supported by this backend".

| Code | Meaning | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0` | Done. | Read back what you wrote before you report it as saved ("Reporting a save", below). A "Note:" line in the output still needs action: report it to the owner, or do what it says. |
| `1` | Error, or the record was not found. | Read the message. It names the cause and usually the fix. Do not run the same command again unchanged. |
| `2` | Validation failure, a refused gate, or a stale `--expect`. | Fix what the message names and run the command again. A refused gate means an approval is missing: ask the owner for it. Never work around a refusal. |
| `3` | Not supported for this tracker or memory backend. | For a GitHub or Jira tracker, the message prints the path of the written instructions for that tracker. Follow them to make the same change on the issue. |
| `4` | Not a Toolkit V2 project. | Skip every work item and memory step and say so in one line. To set the project up, open the `project-setup` skill. |

`toolkit: command not found` means this computer cannot reach the command.
The `project-setup` skill fixes that.

## Reporting a save

- Save each settled answer before moving on, then read it back. A command
  that exits `0` is not proof by itself.
- A write failed: lead the reply with "Not saved". Name what was not saved
  and where it should go, and keep the text so it can be saved later.
- "Saved but not verified" in the output means the write happened and the
  read-back failed. The message names the first part that differs. Lead the
  reply with "Saved but not verified", say which part, and read the record
  back to judge it.

## Reading output and updating what you read

- Add `--json` when you need to read the output field by field, for example
  a record's `version`.
- `--expect <version>` tells the command which version of a record you read.
  The command refuses the save (exit `2`) when the record changed since then,
  so you never overwrite a newer edit. Read it again, merge, and save with the
  new version. `toolkit memory focus`, `toolkit memory glossary`, and
  `toolkit memory save` take it. `--expect absent` says it must not exist
  yet: a new record, or a project with no focus yet.

## Right and wrong examples

1. Two reads.
   - Wrong: `toolkit work list && toolkit work show WI-004`
   - Right: `toolkit work list`, then, as a second command,
     `toolkit work show WI-004`.
2. A history note that quotes the owner, with an apostrophe in his words.
   - Wrong: ``toolkit work history WI-004 --note "Owner said: it's ready, `ship it`"``
     (double quotes: the shell runs the words between the backticks as a
     command and saves its output in their place).
   - Right in Claude Code:
     `toolkit work history WI-004 --note 'Owner said: "it'\''s ready, ship it"'`
   - Right in Codex:
     `toolkit work history WI-004 --note 'Owner said: "it’s ready, ship it"'`
   - The prefix is `Owner said:`, which has no apostrophe to escape.
3. Section text in Codex.
   - Wrong: `cat > /tmp/overview.md <<'EOF' ... EOF && toolkit work edit WI-004 --section 'Overview' --set-file /tmp/overview.md`
     (one shell command, a heredoc, and a fixed file name).
   - Right: `toolkit work edit WI-004 --section 'Overview' --text '<text>'`
4. A change to a work item's header.
   - Wrong: `sed -i '' 's/^stage: .*/stage: 04-solution-design/' .work-items/WI-004/WORK-ITEM.md`
   - Right: `toolkit work set WI-004 --stage 04-solution-design --note '<why>'`
5. Toolkit commands from a script.
   - Wrong: `for id in WI-001 WI-002; do toolkit work show $id; done`
   - Right: `toolkit work show WI-001`, then `toolkit work show WI-002`, each
     as its own command.

# WI-001: Build slug command with max option — solution design

**Requirements:** WI-001  
**Design status:** Proposed  
**Requirements checked:** WI-001, R-01 and R-02, 2026-09-28  
**Last updated:** 2026-09-28

## What this design solves

Mike runs `node bin/slug.js "Hello World!"` to get a slug he can paste into his blog. The command also accepts `--max` to limit the output. It prints one slug and a newline on success, or an error and exit code 1 for the invalid cases in R-01 and R-02. The design covers this command only.

## Requirements and design readiness

R-01 and R-02 are approved and ready to design from. The stated examples and failure cases are explicit. Behavior for scripts beyond the accented Latin example is not separately specified; both options preserve letters and numbers from other scripts rather than discarding valid title content.

| R-01 — Turn a title into a slug | Finalized | Both options normalize text, form hyphen-separated words, and reject an empty result | None for approved checks |

| Type | Constraint or assumption | Source and status | Effect on the design |

## Design options

### Option A — One command file

#### Approach

Put argument parsing and slug conversion in `bin/slug.js`. Use Node.js string normalization and Unicode-aware regular expressions. Add a CLI test file that runs the command as a child process. This keeps a small command in one source file.

#### End-to-end behavior

1. Mike passes one quoted title and optionally `--max` followed by a positive whole number.
2. The command checks the arguments, normalizes accents, converts runs of non-letter and non-number characters to hyphens, lowercases the result, and trims edge hyphens.
3. If a maximum was supplied, it cuts the slug at that many characters and removes a trailing hyphen. It prints the result with a newline. Invalid `--max` or a title yielding no letters or numbers prints an error to stderr and exits 1.

| Requirement | Build or reuse | Why it meets the requirement | How to check it |

- **Integrations:** Node.js process arguments, stdout, stderr, and exit code.
- **Operations:** Run directly with Node.js; revert the command file if needed.

| Tradeoff or risk | Likelihood and effect | Mitigation or owner decision |

# Planning and building a work item

The Roadmap and Tasks formats, tracking setup, and the build rules for
`work-on` stages 06 to 08.

## Contents

1. Roadmap and tasks
2. The Roadmap format
3. The Tasks format
4. Status words and ticking a task
5. Tracking setup (stage 07)
6. Building (stage 08)
7. Keeping the item current while building
8. Checklist before stopping

## 1. Roadmap and tasks

- The Roadmap is an ordered list of phases from where the item stands to the
  finished result. Name phases to fit the work. "Phase" (`P1`) is the item's
  plan; "stage" (`08-build`) is the lifecycle. Never mix the two words.
- Build the phases from the approved design's "Build and verification plan"
  (its Technical sequence and Acceptance checks) and the chosen option's
  Build order. With no design (a small item that skipped design with a
  recorded reason), build them from the requirements.
- A sub-item that inherits its parent's approved design is planned from the
  parent's design: `toolkit work design <parent-id>`.
- Each phase has one or more tasks, one or more sub-items, or both.
- Keep detail in proportion. A one-hour fix needs one phase with one or two
  tasks.
- Link sources; do not copy them. A task names the `R-xx` it implements and
  the design section it follows.

## 2. The Roadmap format

The table keeps these columns in every tracker. The phase name follows an em
dash, as in the template.

```markdown
A phase is complete when its tasks are complete and its exit result has been checked.

| Phase | Outcome | Status | Exit result | Sub-items |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 — CSV export button | The export button creates a file | In Progress | The file opens in Excel with every column | None. |
| P2 — Large exports | Exports over 10,000 rows finish | Not Started | A 50,000-row export finishes in under a minute | WI-015 |
```

## 3. The Tasks format

Each phase gets a `###` heading with the same phase id and name as its
Roadmap row. Each task field (`**Work:**`, `**Deliverable:**`,
`**Done when:**`, `**Depends on:**`) starts its own line, and every line of a
task but the last ends with two spaces, which Markdown reads as a line break.
Never run the fields together on one line.

```markdown
### P1 — CSV export button

- [ ] **P1-T01 — Add the export endpoint** · In Progress  
  **Work:** Add the endpoint that streams the report rows as CSV (R-01, design Technical sequence step 1).  
  **Deliverable:** The endpoint and its tests.  
  **Done when:** The endpoint test passes and a manual export opens in Excel.  
  **Depends on:** None.
- [ ] **P1-T02 — Add the Export button** · Not Started  
  **Work:** Add the button that calls the endpoint (R-01).  
  **Deliverable:** The button and its test.  
  **Done when:** Clicking Export downloads the file.  
  **Depends on:** P1-T01.
```

Save both sections with the section command (`work-item-format.md`,
"Changing one section"):

```text
toolkit work edit <id> --section Roadmap --set-file <file>
toolkit work edit <id> --section Tasks --set-file <file>
```

## 4. Status words and ticking a task

- Phase status: Not Started, In Progress, Done (Cancelled for a phase that
  was dropped). Use no other word, such as "Planned".
- Task status: Not Started, In Progress, Done, Cancelled.
- From stage 07 on, `toolkit work validate` warns when the Roadmap has no
  phase table, when Tasks has no checkbox lines, and when a template example
  row or task is left.
- Tick a task (`- [x]`, status Done) only with evidence: the test result
  line, the commit, or what the owner saw.
- A done or cancelled task is not reopened. Add a new task instead.
- A task whose "Done when" names the owner (for example "the owner confirms
  the wording") is not ticked by the agent. It becomes an Open Questions row
  with `owner` as who decides.
- A phase that a sub-item delivers lists the sub-item id in its Sub-items
  column. Finishing the sub-item does not finish or approve the parent.
- When the item is finished, every phase it completed says Done.

## 5. Tracking setup (stage 07)

Only what the item needs:

- **Branch and worktree** for code work: the worktree
  `.claude/worktrees/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>` on the branch
  `claude/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>`, as the project's
  `.claude/rules/shared-repository-work.md` says. `toolkit work show <id>`
  prints the exact names. For WI-007:
  `git worktree add .claude/worktrees/wi-007-csv-export -b claude/wi-007-csv-export`
  In Codex this Git write needs the owner's approval and escalated
  permissions (`git-rules.md`).
- **Salesforce projects:** the item's deployment folder
  `delivery/deployment/<work-item-id>-<short-name>/`, copied from
  `delivery/deployment/work-item-deployment-template/` and kept current by
  `sf-component-tracker`.
- **A test plan**, when the checks need more than the item's acceptance
  checks (several scenarios, a manual check, or a release): `work-check`
  writes it, in `tests/` on the item's branch.
- **Sub-items** for phases that own real scope: open `work-organize`.

## 6. Building (stage 08)

- Work on the item's own branch and worktree. Never on the default branch.
- One task at a time, in the order the Depends on lines allow.
- Commit with files staged by name and a plain message. No `Co-Authored-By`
  line naming an AI and no "Generated with" line (`git-rules.md`).
- With a team recorded by `work-delegate`: one `builder` agent per
  independent task, each with its own files. The main agent merges each
  builder's branch into the item's branch, checks the tests still pass, then
  ticks the task. Builders never change the work item.
- In Codex, a builder gets no worktree by itself. Before each one starts, the
  main agent makes its worktree and branch and names the folder in the
  brief; with approvals off, one builder at a time in the item's own worktree
  (`helpers.md`, section 2, "Codex builders").
- Tests go with each task. A check that could not run is reported as not
  run, never as passed.
- Salesforce: run `sf-component-tracker` after each metadata change. Anything
  that changes production data goes through `sf-data-change`; agents never
  write production data.
- The build shows a requirement is wrong or missing: stop that task, add an
  Open Questions row, and open `work-requirements`. Do not build around it.
- The build shows the design does not work: record it in the design's Notes
  and open `solution-design` for a design change.

## 7. Keeping the item current while building

After each task:

- tick it with evidence;
- update Overview Current position and Next action;
- add a history note only when something changed the plan.

The owner may edit the record while you build. Read the section again right
before you change it.

## 8. Checklist before stopping

Before the reply that ends a session with work unfinished:

- [ ] Overview Current position and Next action say where things stand.
- [ ] Notes > Resume here says exactly where to pick up.
- [ ] `waiting_on` is true: `owner` only while a question for him is open.
- [ ] One history note says what changed in this session.
- [ ] `toolkit work validate <id>` is clean.
- [ ] The current focus names the item and its real next step
      (`current-focus.md`).
- [ ] The reply ends with the one question for the owner, or the exact words
      that continue ("Say 'keep going' and I'll build P1.").

The `handoff` skill does this when the owner is clearing context.

# Git rules for Toolkit V2 skills

Purpose: the Git rules every Toolkit V2 skill follows when it makes a branch,
commits, merges, pushes, or removes a worktree, in Claude Code and in Codex.

## Contents

- Look before the first Git write
- Branch and worktree names for a work item
- Staging and committing
- No AI credit
- The Git-ignored toolkit folders
- A project with no remote
- The merge-safety check
- A merge that stops on a conflict
- Git writes in Codex
- Checklist: one commit
- Examples

## Look before the first Git write

Other sessions may work in the same repository at the same time. Before the
first Git write in a session, run each of these on its own:

```text
git worktree list
git status
git remote
```

- `git remote` prints nothing: the project has no remote. Read "A project
  with no remote" below before any fetch, pull, push, or pull request.
- An unknown worktree, a branch that moved, or a change this session did not
  make means another session is working. Do not change it. Tell the owner.
- The shared primary checkout is the first entry `git worktree list` prints.
  In it, never switch branches, reset, rebase, or stash.
- Never commit, push, rebase, or delete another session's branch, and never
  commit its uncommitted changes, even when they look finished.

## Branch and worktree names for a work item

A work item's code work happens in its own worktree, on its own branch.

| Part | Form | Example for `WI-007`, "CSV export" |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Branch | `claude/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>` | `claude/wi-007-csv-export` |
| Worktree folder | `.claude/worktrees/<prefix>-<number>-<slug>` | `.claude/worktrees/wi-007-csv-export` |

- `<prefix>` is the item's own id prefix in lower case: `wi` for `WI-007`,
  `tv2` for `TV2-007`, `acme` for `ACME-007`.
- The session briefing and `merge-and-clean-up` find the item from the id in
  the branch name. A branch named `wi-001-<slug>` for item `TV2-001` is not
  linked to that item.
- Make both with one command:

  ```text
  git worktree add .claude/worktrees/wi-007-csv-export -b claude/wi-007-csv-export
  ```

- Build on the item's branch, never on the default branch.

## Staging and committing

- Stage each path by name. Never run `git add -A`, `git add .`, or
  `git commit -a`: in a shared checkout they take other sessions' files.
- Read the staged file list, then the full staged diff, before the commit.
  Unstage any file this session did not write.

  ```text
  git diff --cached --name-status
  git diff --cached
  ```

- Write a plain commit message that says what changed, in one line when one
  line is enough.

## No AI credit

Nothing committed or published names an AI as an author or a helper:

- no `Co-Authored-By:` line naming an AI (a line naming a real person is
  allowed);
- no "Generated with" line;
- no AI credit in a pull request title or description, a code comment, a file
  header, or release notes.

The pre-tool hook refuses a commit or pull request command that carries such
a line. When it refuses, change the wording. Never commit another way to get
past it.

## The Git-ignored toolkit folders

`.work-items/` and `.memory/` are Git-ignored and live in the main checkout.

- Never commit them, and never force them in with `git add -f`. The hook
  refuses it.
- Never run `git clean -x` or `git clean -X` in the main checkout. It deletes
  both folders, and Git cannot bring them back. The hook refuses it.
- They change only through `toolkit work` and `toolkit memory` commands.
- Their backup is automatic: `toolkit work finish` and the handoff copy them
  to the owner's backup folder (`toolkit handoff-backup` does the same on
  request). `toolkit export --to <folder>` makes a one-off copy.

## A project with no remote

`git remote` prints nothing.

- Never run `git fetch`, `git pull`, or `git push`. A fetch that fails or is
  refused is not a blocker: never report it as one, and never write it into a
  work item.
- There is no pull request. `work-finish` merges the item's branch into the
  default branch locally, after the same approval a pull request merge needs,
  from the main checkout:

  ```text
  git merge --ff-only claude/wi-007-csv-export
  ```

  Then it adds the history note "No remote: merged locally into
  <default branch>."
- The fast-forward fails when the default branch moved on after the item's
  branch was made (for example another item's local merge). Merge the default
  branch into the item's branch in the item's worktree (`git merge main`, with
  the real default branch name), run the item's checks again, then run the
  fast-forward again.
- Documents are committed on the local default branch. `publish-docs` does
  this by itself.
- `merge-and-clean-up`, `pull-latest`, and `reset-to-remote` have nothing to
  do. Say so in one line.

## The merge-safety check

Before any merge into the default branch, check that it cannot overwrite
another session's uncommitted work in the primary checkout. With a remote,
fetch first so the comparison uses the remote's default branch.

```text
git diff --name-only main...claude/wi-007-csv-export
git -C <primary checkout> status --porcelain
```

Use the real default branch name, and `origin/<default branch>` when there is
a remote. A file in both lists: stop, name exactly those files, and let the
owner decide whether to commit, stash, or wait. Never touch the primary
checkout's changes yourself.

## A merge that stops on a conflict

1. Read both sides of each conflicting file. When the right result is not
   clear from the two sides, stop and ask the owner.
2. Stage each resolved file by name.
3. Commit with a message you write:

   ```text
   git commit -m 'Merge main into claude/wi-007-csv-export: keep both export formats'
   ```

Never run `git commit --no-edit` after a conflict: it keeps Git's
"# Conflicts:" lines in the message.

## Git writes in Codex

Codex's sandbox keeps `.git/` read-only. Every command that writes `.git/`
fails inside it: `git add`, `commit`, `merge`, `fetch`, `pull`, `push`,
`switch`, `checkout`, `restore`, `rm`, `mv`, `stash`, `cherry-pick`,
`revert`, `rebase`, `reset`, `update-ref`, `git worktree add`, `remove`,
`move`, `prune`, and `repair`, and `git branch -d`, `-D`, `-m`, `-c`, and
`-f`. The project's
`.codex/rules/toolkit.rules` makes Codex ask the owner before each one. A `gh`
call that needs the network is also refused inside the sandbox.

Reading commands (`git status`, `git log`, `git diff`, `git show`,
`git branch --list`, `git worktree list`) run inside the sandbox as usual.

For each Git write in Codex:

- [ ] Run the Git command alone, as its own command: not joined to another
      command with `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and not from a script.
- [ ] Say in one line what the command does, before Codex asks the owner.
- [ ] Ask for escalated permissions: set `sandbox_permissions` to
      `require_escalated`, with a one-line reason that says what the command
      does ("Create the worktree for WI-002 on its own branch."). An approval
      without escalation still runs the command inside the sandbox, where it
      fails on `.git/index.lock`.
- [ ] Codex refused it without asking ("approval required by policy", or
      "AskForApproval is set to Never"): this session cannot ask. Stop that
      step, show the owner the exact command, and ask him to approve it in an
      interactive session or run it in a terminal. Set the work item waiting
      on the owner. It is not an outside blocker.

Never work around a refusal: no nested `git clone` of the project, no copy of
`.git/`, no script that runs Git for you, and no building on the default
branch instead of the item's branch. The `publish-docs` script is not such a
script: it is that skill's own tool. Run it alone with escalated permissions,
like any other Git write.

## Checklist: one commit

```text
- [ ] In the right worktree, on the right branch (git branch --show-current)
- [ ] Each path staged by name
- [ ] Staged list read: only this session's files, no .work-items/ or .memory/
- [ ] Full staged diff read
- [ ] Plain message with no AI credit line
- [ ] Codex: each Git command run alone, with escalated permissions
```

## Examples

Right: stage by name, read the list, commit.

```text
git add src/export.js tests/export.test.js
git diff --cached --name-status
git commit -m 'Add CSV export for invoices'
```

Wrong: `git add -A && git commit -m 'wip'`. It stages other sessions' files,
and in Codex the joined command runs inside the sandbox and fails.

Wrong: a message whose last line is a `Co-Authored-By:` trailer naming an AI
model. The hook refuses it. Remove the line and commit again.

Right, no remote: after the owner approves the result and the merge,

```text
git merge --ff-only claude/wi-007-csv-export
```

run from the main checkout, then the history note "No remote: merged locally
into main."

Right, Codex: `git commit -m 'Add CSV export for invoices'` run alone, with
`sandbox_permissions` set to `require_escalated` and the reason "Commit the
CSV export files for WI-007 on its branch."
# Sizing a request and routing an item

How `work-on` decides between a quick edit, a logged item, and a worked item,
which type to give it, and which skill continues it.

## Contents

1. Three sizes of request
2. Owner messages and the right action
3. Choosing the type
4. Routing by where the item stands
5. Several items at once
6. Project roadmap units

## 1. Three sizes of request

- **Quick edit, no item.** One sitting, no choice for the owner, no change to
  behavior recorded in `requirements/`, nothing bound for production. Do it
  and report it in one line.
- **Log only.** The owner says "later", "backlog", "park that", "not now", or
  "log a bug". Check the list for a duplicate, create the item at
  `01-discovery` with his exact words as the Starting request, reply
  "Logged as WI-014 (bug, backlog). Not started." and stop.
- **Work item.** Everything else. "New work", "track", "work item", or "done
  properly" always makes an item. A request that grows past a quick edit
  while you work becomes an item then, with his words as the Starting
  request.

Never make a work item for project setup. Setup steps the owner must do go in
the reply. Only a step `toolkit doctor` checks (trusting the hooks in Codex
`/hooks`, `ntn login`) also goes in the current focus under "Waiting on the
owner", marked as a setup step, and leaves it once doctor stops reporting it.
"Start a new session" goes in the reply only.

A deliverable the owner named without saying what it should say or do ("write
a short project brief"): create the item, add the content question as `Q-01`
with the item waiting on him, and ask it in the reply before building.
Never invent the content.

## 2. Owner messages and the right action

| The owner says | Right action |
| --- | --- |
| "Fix the typo in the README heading." | Quick edit. Fix it, say what changed in one line. No item. |
| "What does the export function do?" | Answer the question. No item. |
| "Log a bug: the export drops the last row. Not now." | Log only: check for a duplicate, create a `bug` item at `01-discovery` with his words, reply "Logged as WI-014 (bug, backlog). Not started." |
| "Add a CSV export to the monthly report." | Work item, type `build`. Create it, then route: requirements are not approved, so open `work-requirements`. |
| "Write a short project brief." | Work item, type `task`. Add `Q-01` "What should the brief cover?", set it waiting on the owner, ask the question. |
| "Keep going." (no item named) | Continue this worktree's item, or the item the current focus says the next session starts with, or the one `toolkit work next` recommends. Say which in one line. |
| "ok" (and this chat asked him nothing) | Not "keep going". Start no work; ask what he wants. |
| "Ask me questions first, then build it." | Create the item and open `work-requirements` for the interview. Never batch questions here. |
| "Put it in the backlog and I'll tell you when." | Log only. |
| "WI-007" or "resume WI-007" | Read WI-007 and route it by where it stands (section 4). |

## 3. Choosing the type

- Pick the closest type from `toolkit work lifecycle`.
- A change to what the product does, to Salesforce metadata (`force-app/`),
  or to anything bound for production is `build`, never `task`, even when it
  looks small. A change to data is `data-load`.
- `build` and `data-load` need the owner's requirements approval before stage
  03. The CLI refuses a later stage without it.
- A `task` with no open choices may skip the requirements approval and go
  straight to planning. Put the reason in a history note.

## 4. Routing by where the item stands

The "Continue with" line of `toolkit work show <id>` is the default. The
item's real state decides. Go down the table in order and take the first row
that matches: the owner's waiting decisions come first, then the delivery
offer, then the stage. Say the route in one line.

| Where the item stands | Open | One-line announcement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `waiting_on: owner` | `work-decide` (ask that one question first; keep working on anything it does not block) | "WI-012 is waiting for your OK on the requirements." |
| The agent to-do "Make the agent-led delivery offer" for this item (the briefing and `toolkit work decisions` list it for a big top-level item at stages 03 to 07 that still has `delivery: not-offered`), or the owner hands the goal over ("you drive") | `work-delegate`, and build nothing until he answers | "WI-012 needs your delivery choice; opening work-delegate." |
| Requirements not approved and type `build` or `data-load` | `work-requirements` | "WI-012 needs requirements first; opening work-requirements." |
| The owner asks to change, add, or drop a requirement, at any stage | `work-requirements` | "That changes R-02; opening work-requirements." |
| Requirements approved, more than one reasonable way to build, no approved design | `solution-design` | "WI-012 needs a design; opening solution-design." |
| Requirements approved, one clear way to build, no design | Stay here: say the approach in the final reply ("One way to build this: <approach>. I'll build it that way; say 'design first' to stop me.") and put the reason in a history note | |
| Too big for one build | `work-organize` (split, stage 05) | "WI-012 is too big for one build; opening work-organize." |
| Design approved, or a sub-item that inherits the parent's approved design | Stay here: plan (stage 06) | |
| Stages 09 to 11 | `work-check` | "WI-012 is in testing; opening work-check." |
| Stages 12 to 14, or result approved | `work-finish` | "WI-012 is approved; opening work-finish." |
| Done or Cancelled | Nothing. Reopen only when the owner asks: `toolkit work set <id> --stage <s> --reopen` | |

- Stages may be skipped, repeated, or revisited. Record a one-line reason
  when a move is not obvious.
- An item that changes committed files always goes through stage 07 (its own
  worktree). Never build on the default branch.
- A worktree whose branch names an item (`claude/wi-007-csv-export`) belongs
  to that item. The briefing says so. Work on that item there.
- Never ask the owner which stage an item is in.

## 5. Several items at once

- Read each item's record before recommending an order. Say what can go
  ahead on its own, what depends on another outcome, and which one decision
  would unblock the most work.
- Each item has one main session that changes it. Other sessions return
  findings to it instead of editing the same record.
- Worktrees keep code apart; they do not keep shared environments apart.
  Check shared orgs, databases, and releases before two items change the same
  one.

## 6. Project roadmap units

`PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` holds the project's phases (`P01`) and deliverable-sized
work units, each naming its work item id. Item detail stays in the tracker.

- When a new item is one of those units, write its id into the unit and save
  the file with `publish-docs`.
- An item's own phases (`P1`) are a different thing. They live in the item's
  Roadmap section.
